extracted.intended_audience: general readers and analysts of satirical fiction (Victorian social satire)
extracted.subtask_description: Close reading / extraction of the social-normative claims and prescriptive passages in a satirical Victorian novel (Butler's Erewhon), focusing on its rules, procedures and criticisms about birth, education, money, and family life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural conditions for an unborn to become born
rubrics_metrics.description: Before an unborn may leave their world they must go before the magistrate, sign an affidavit of desire to quit, be read a long list of conditions, and accept them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Principal points of the conditions (as extracted): they must take a potion which destroys memory and sense of identity; go into the world helpless and without a will of their own; draw lots for their dispositions before they go and accept them for better or worse; have no choice in the matter of the body allotted to them; be simply allotted by chance and without appeal to two people whom it is their business to find and pester until they adopt them. The affidavit/magistrate ritual and the potion are mandatory procedural steps; only the most foolish unborn consent given the risks described.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lecture-style arguments discouraging the unborn from choosing birth
rubrics_metrics.description: A formal set of reasons presented to dissuade an unborn from being born, framed as sober warnings about the risks and burdens of embodied life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arguments include: being born is a felony/capital crime with possible future punishment; the brevity and deterioration of earthly pleasures (pleasures concentrated in youth, decrepit old age follows); risk of being born to wicked, silly, unsympathetic, or domineering parents; being treated as chattel or property; the possibility of ingrained ingratitude from offspring; loss of present bliss and acquisition of burdensome free will; necessity to live by weighing considerations and often erring; the thought that many people would not choose to be born again if offered. Practical advice given if an abortive memory returns: 'fly... to the haven of your present and immediate duty, taking shelter incessantly in the work which you have in hand.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Ontological description of the unborn and their limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: The unborn are pictured as pure, gaseous, anthropomorphic souls without flesh, blood, or warmth, living in unsubstantial cities, eating a thin ambrosial sustenance, able to read thoughts and observe mankind, numerous and arriving full-grown from unknown planets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences explained: they never die while remaining unborn (only death is leaving for our world); they can only depart by taking the steps for arrival here (i.e., suicide); most who are sufficiently restless or bored are driven to risk birth despite the uncertain and hazardous conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural selection argument against prescience
rubrics_metrics.description: A cautionary social observation that a race which knew the future better than the past perished from misery within a year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inference given: were any unborn to be too prescient now, natural selection would cull them before they could transmit that faculty, because prescience is peace-destroying and tends to cause misery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critique of 'schools of Unreason' and preference for practical education
rubrics_metrics.description: Compulsory, hypothetical, or theoretical schooling (the 'schools of Unreason') is portrayed as producing years of incapacity and directing children into false channels instead of giving them the means to earn a living.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy-like recommendations: provide only basic state-aided instruction in reading, writing, and arithmetic; end compulsory state education beyond basics; have children begin (with safeguards against overwork) to acquire the rudiments of the art by which they will earn their living in actual workshops under practicing masters rather than in cloistered technical schools; practical apprenticeship and early earning are preferable to prolonged hypothetical instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incentivize early self-support: tax parents of non-earning children
rubrics_metrics.description: A proposed fiscal remedy: impose a tax upon parents whose children are not earning a competence by age twenty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: such a tax would motivate parents to have their children begin earning early, producing independent young adults, reducing family strain (and the resort to infanticide), and improving parent-child relations. The expected effect is that parents would take steps to ensure their children acquire practical skills and enter productive life sooner.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exempt extraordinary wealth from taxation as recognition of social contribution
rubrics_metrics.description: A social valuation rule: persons who have made very large fortunes (example threshold given: over £20,000 a year) are exempted from taxation because they are regarded as a 'work of art' and 'too precious to be meddled with.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Justification provided in text: extreme riches are taken as evidence of having done what mankind wanted; money is called 'the symbol of duty' and 'the sacrament of having done for mankind that which mankind wanted.' This is presented as an Erewhonian maxim, used to praise wealth and to defend tax exemption for the very rich.

rubrics_metrics.name: Argument that want of money can be as harmful as love of money
rubrics_metrics.description: A normative claim about moral economy: opposing money to culture is fallacious; earning an honourable independence supports culture, while lack of money (want of money) is as much a root of evil as the love of money.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied advice: for many individuals their proper duty is to secure income and respectable independence (even to accumulate wealth) rather than to adopt ascetic giving that renders them ineffective; poverty can worsen moral and social outcomes and make cultivated sensibilities burdensome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parental conduct: remember your own youth and practise forbearance
rubrics_metrics.description: Advice to parents that if they remembered how they felt when young and behaved towards their children as they wished their parents had behaved, family affection and relations would improve.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text frames this as a simple axiom rarely practised; good and patient parental behaviour is said to produce reciprocal affection and long-term familial pleasure. The counterpoint is the prevalence of poor practice: many parents are unable to put this into practice, causing unhappy family relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satirical proposals about age relations and corporal chastisement
rubrics_metrics.description: A reported radical proposal: alternate the authority of age and youth week by week (drawing the line at thirty-five) and permit the young to inflict corporal chastisement on the old to keep them 'corrigible.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as an extreme and probably impractical idea—its mention functions as satire evidencing 'the utter perversion of the Erewhonian mind.' The passage uses this to highlight how mistaken political/educational schemes can become when taken to absurdity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Colleges of Unreason as a social fetish that makes children useless
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'Colleges of Unreason' are institutions of which respectable families feel compelled to be devotees (Ydgrun-worship), yet they allegedly render students less fit for practical life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique notes these colleges cost time and money, instil hypothetical lore not practical skill, and thus victimize both parents (by expense) and children (by making them less capable of earning). The narrator calls them cloister-life opposed to workshop learning and implies they contribute to social ills like infanticide and family strain.
